input.question: If people who have been bitten or stung by some insects such as fire ants have a higher risk of developing an allergy to them, then how do long term treatments such as whole body extract immunotherapy (slowly exposing the body to the venom) work?
input.ground_truth: Exposing the body to anything foreign in small harmless enough doses will allow the body to develop white blood cells responsible for removing foreign material from the body. Part of the reason that people can develop allergies to toxins is that their immune system reaponds “too well” to the attack. There are suppressors in place to regulate inflammation and damage, but if they are shut off then the body responds violently. The reason that people who are stung by some insects have a greater chance of becoming allergic is because oftentimes, the insects are not trying to administer the toxin in a damage free concentration. The body responds quickly and can forego suppressor function but you run the risk of developing to strong of a reaction.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: If people who have been bitten or stung by some insects such as fire ants have a higher risk of developing an allergy to them, then how do long term treatments such as whole body extract immunotherapy (slowly exposing the body to the venom) work?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you got a tiny poke from a fire ant, and now your body doesn’t like fire ants anymore. It gets scared and might have a big reaction if it sees one again, like a big allergy.

Now, doctors have a special way to help your body get used to the fire ant’s poke, so it’s not so scared anymore. It’s like when you are scared of a puppy at first, but if you see the puppy a little bit every day and nothing bad happens, you start to not be scared anymore.

With the special medicine called immunotherapy, doctors give you a tiny, tiny bit of the fire ant’s “poke stuff” (called venom) at first, so tiny that it doesn’t hurt you. Then, over a long time, they give you a little bit more each time. This helps your body learn, “Hey, this isn’t so bad!” So, when you really get poked by a fire ant later, your body doesn’t get so scared and doesn’t have a big allergy reaction.

It’s like teaching your body to be friends with the fire ant’s poke!
